rv.q: What was once a spooky and balletic spectacle of 1980s excess, best known for the hit song “Memory” and purring chorines crawling on the seats, is now a glitter bomb of euphoric pandemonium.

After an already-legendary Off Broadway debut at the Perelman Arts Center in 2024, this production—under the chosen name Cats: The Jellicle Ball–has now re-inhabited Broadway, where it remains a categorical triumph.
It was a beautiful suggestion of the show’s open-armed sensibility, a way of lovingly glorifying both the past and the present, and, fingers crossed, the future . . . now and forever.
Because what we do hear is spectacular.
“Cats: The Jellicle Ball” just might become the next much-needed, must-see touring show from the House of Broadway.
What those outsiders have achieved with The Jellicle Ball is a revival in the fullest sense of the word.
Because there’s simply no topping the sheer euphoria onstage at the Broadhurst Theatre.
This Ball is not just a remembrance of things past—it points a way forward, to a more fabulous future.
It’s that the show is now imbued with a tangible emotional thrust, bringing to life what was dormant but always there.

Jellicle Ball is so flat-out fun it smothers every slight ever suffered by Lloyd Webber’s 1980s mega-musical, from snickers layered into Tony Kushner’s America and Paul Rudnick’s Jeffrey to the travesty of that uncanny valley film in 2019.
The spectacle of Jellicle Ball is intoxicating for all who enter and give themselves over to the glamor.
This irresistible revival isn’t your grandma’s Cats; but in many ways, it is the truest version of the musical yet.

Artistically, the fresh interpretation not only offers the possibility of a renewed life and a new audience for this overly familiar 45-year-old show; it suggests how the art form as a whole can be reinvigorated.
Only when William Waldrop’s orchestrations riff by imposing a bump, stomp and grind rhythm to the original score does this “Cats” spring alive to grow painted claws.
Not only is this Cats different from any you have ever seen before, it is the most dynamic musical show to be seen in New York right now.
This production proves the material can hold radically different visions.
There’s no denying how much fun this production is – and how even a flawed and dated show can find a path to rebirth via Eliot’s vaunted Heaviside Layer.
